c.tagline: A tri-border Amazon gateway where Colombia, Brazil, and Peru meet along the world's largest river

taxi.fareNote: Moto-taxis are the fastest way around the small town center

avoid.reason: Avoid the unlit riverfront port area and the border backstreets toward Tabatinga late at night, where smuggling-related crime occurs.
Book jungle excursions only with registered guides and steer clear of remote river stretches at night due to trafficking activity.

hood_desc: The compact commercial core around Santander Park, with the cathedral, most hotels, and restaurants; the natural base for exploring the region.
The Amazon River waterfront, where cargo boats, tour operators, and river-market vendors set the rhythm of daily life.
A rainforest reserve just outside town offering canopy walkways and overnight jungle lodges without a long river journey.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

food.name: Pirarucú
food.desc: The Amazon's giant air-breathing fish, firm and almost meaty; grilled in banana leaf or torn into golden chicharrones with lime and cassava.

places.name: Tierras Amazónicas
places.note: Repeatedly called the best place in town for Amazon dishes; the pirarucú chicharrones are the order.

places.name: Restaurante Flotante Pirarucú
places.note: Floating restaurant on the river serving local fish with the water right below you.

places.name: Las Margaritas
places.note: Buffet upriver whose crisp pirarucú fritters are its signature.

food.name: Gamitana a la parrilla
food.desc: Sweet-fleshed river fish scored and grilled whole over wood, or stewed; served with fried plantain, rice and a sharp chilli-and-lime ají.

places.name: Tierras Amazónicas
places.note: Gamitana stew and ceviches sit beside the pirarucú on the menu.

places.name: Numae Bistró
places.note: River-view kitchen doing grilled fish and meat with forest-fruit sides.

places.name: Mercado Municipal food counters
places.note: Morning fish market where the day's catch is cooked at the stalls behind.

food.name: Casabe and fariña
food.desc: Bitter cassava pressed, dried and baked into brittle casabe discs, or toasted into coarse fariña grains scattered over everything like a condiment.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Leticia
places.note: Indigenous producers sell casabe rounds and sacks of fariña by the kilo.

places.name: Mundo Amazónico
places.note: Reserve restaurant that explains and serves the cassava staples in context.

places.name: Tierras Amazónicas
places.note: Served as the standard accompaniment to the fish plates.

food.name: Tacacho con cecina
food.desc: Green plantain roasted, mashed with pork fat and rolled into balls, served with salted smoked pork; a triple-frontier dish borrowed from Peru.

places.name: Restaurante Tucupí
places.note: Comfortable, cheap and family-run; good for the cross-border Amazon staples.

places.name: Mercado Municipal food counters
places.note: Where Peruvian and Brazilian dishes appear alongside Colombian ones.

places.name: Tabatinga border eateries
places.note: Walkable from Leticia; the frontier is where the three cuisines meet.

food.name: Patarashca (fish in bijao leaf)
food.desc: River fish packed with garlic, herbs and chilli into a bijao leaf parcel and cooked over embers so it steams in its own juices.

places.name: Mundo Amazónico
places.note: Set inside a nature reserve; food served surrounded by forest and birdsong.

places.name: Las Margaritas
places.note: Traditional preparations done properly in the quiet town upriver.

food.name: Mojojoy (palm grubs)
food.desc: Fat aguaje-palm larvae, skewered and grilled until the skin crisps; a genuine Amazon delicacy that tastes closer to bacon than you expect.

places.name: Tierras Amazónicas
places.note: Long noted by visitors as the place in Leticia to try mojojoy properly cooked.

places.name: Mercado Municipal de Leticia
places.note: Sold live by indigenous vendors and grilled to order at the stalls.

food.name: Amazon fruit juices
food.desc: Copoazú, arazá, camu camu and açaí blended fresh: sharp, floral, unlike anything in a supermarket, and served in glasses the size of jugs.

places.name: Mercado Municipal juice stands
places.note: Cheapest and widest range; fruit changes with what came downriver that week.

places.name: Numae Bistró
places.note: Natural juices and forest-fruit salads with a river view.

places.name: Parque Santander kiosks
places.note: Juice carts around the central park, busiest at the evening parrot roost.

food.name: Masato de yuca
food.desc: Traditional cassava drink of the Tikuna and neighbouring peoples: cooked yuca mashed and lightly fermented into a thick, tangy, milky brew.

places.name: Mundo Amazónico
places.note: Serves and explains indigenous preparations as part of the reserve visit.

places.name: Puerto Nariño community kitchens
places.note: Upriver town where Tikuna families still make masato the traditional way.

landmarks: Parque Santander
Leticia's central plaza, transformed each dusk when thousands of screeching pericos (parakeets) swirl in to roost in its trees.
Amazon River excursions
The city's raison d'être: boat journeys on the world's mightiest river, gateway to flooded forests, riverside villages and three-country panoramas.
Mundo Amazónico Ethnobotanical Park
A well-run reserve outside town with guided trails through medicinal gardens, an aquarium of Amazon fish and indigenous cultural demonstrations.
Museo Etnográfico de Leticia
The Banco de la República's small, excellent museum introducing the cosmology, featherwork and ritual objects of Amazonian indigenous peoples.
Tres Fronteras (Three Borders)
The point where Colombia, Brazil and Peru meet on the Amazon; strolling into Brazilian Tabatinga or boating to Peru's Santa Rosa is a rite of passage.
Catedral Nuestra Señora de la Paz
Leticia's modest modern cathedral near the port, a cool, quiet counterpoint to the border town's sweltering street bustle.
Flor Lagoon
A swimming lagoon dotted with giant Victoria water lilies and parrots on the edge of Leticia, with a small bar for cooling off after the jungle heat.
Acuarios Etuena
The first aquarium in the region to display native Amazon rainforest fish species, a small but distinctive stop for river wildlife close to town.
Yahuarcaca Lakes
A wetland system of oxbow lakes just outside Leticia, popular for kayaking and birdwatching among flooded forest close to the Amazon River.
Puerto de Leticia
The Amazon River port that is Leticia's lifeline to Peru, Brazil and the jungle interior, its position shifting with the river's seasonal water levels.

train.note: There is no railway anywhere in the Colombian Amazon. Leticia is not connected by road to the rest of Colombia at all - access is by air from Bogotá or by river.

bus.note: No coach routes - there are no roads out of Leticia. You can walk or take a moto-taxi across the open border into Tabatinga in Brazil, which is effectively the same town, and Santa Rosa in Peru is a short boat ride away. All longer journeys are by river or air.

intl.to: Iquitos (Peru) - fast boat, ~10-12 hr, or slow boat, ~2-3 days - departs from Santa Rosa
intl.op: Transtur / Golfinho fast-boat operators — tickets at the Leticia riverfront agencies

intl.to: Manaus (Brazil) - slow boat from Tabatinga, ~3-4 days downriver
intl.op: Amazon riverboat operators — tickets at the Tabatinga port

ferry.note: The river is the road here, and these are genuine international crossings on the three-way frontier. Boats to Iquitos leave from Santa Rosa on the Peruvian bank; boats to Manaus leave from Tabatinga on the Brazilian side. Get your Colombian exit stamp at Leticia airport and the entry stamp for Peru or Brazil at the corresponding post before boarding - immigration is not done on the boat. Slow boats are hammock-deck affairs taking days; fast boats do Iquitos in a long day.

half.name: Isla de los Micos (Monkey Island)
half.blurb: A river island upstream where troops of squirrel monkeys clamber over delighted visitors amid Amazonian forest.

full.name: Puerto Nariño
full.blurb: A car-free, flower-filled indigenous river town two hours upstream, a model of Amazonian sustainability with a lookout tower over the treetops.

full.name: Lago Tarapoto
full.blurb: A protected lake system near Puerto Nariño where pink river dolphins surface among giant water lilies and flooded forest.

notes.walk: Central Leticia is small and walkable; reaching the rainforest reserves, Monkey Island, or Tabatinga (Brazil) requires a boat, taxi, or short walk across the unmarked border
notes.card: Accepted at larger hotels; cash is essential for markets, boats, and small eateries
notes.safety: Generally safe in the town center; exercise standard caution near the borders and when traveling by boat after dark. Petty theft can occur in markets; most visitors experience no issues traveling with a reputable tour operator.
notes.religion: Christianity (Roman Catholic majority); indigenous spiritual traditions (practiced alongside Christianity in some communities)
notes.langs: Spanish; Portuguese (common due to Brazilian border); indigenous languages (Ticuna and others)
notes.net: Moderate 3G/4G in town, minimal coverage on the river or in the rainforest. Wifi available in most hotels. ~$8-15 for a prepaid tourist SIM. Wifi available in hotels, though speeds are modest. A Claro or Movistar tourist SIM or eSIM.
notes.transit: Moto-taxis and small local buses within town; river boats connect to outlying reserves and villages
notes.transport: Alfredo Vásquez Cobo International Airport (LET), about 10 min from town, with flights from Bogotá. No passenger rail service. No long-distance road connections to the rest of Colombia (surrounded by rainforest and rivers). Riverboats connect Leticia to Iquitos, Peru and other Amazon river towns (multi-day journey). Not applicable for reaching Leticia; local roads within town are limited.

laundry.note: Self-service in big cities; most laundries are staff-run
